text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • First prenatal visit: dating ultrasound; blood count, blood group and antibody screen, rubella immunity, hepatitis B surface antigen, HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis C tests; urine culture; metabolic panel and urinalysis because of vomiting; influenza vaccine; folic acid 0.4 mg daily in place of the iron-containing prenatal vitamin while nausea lasts
  • Nausea and vomiting, step by step: small frequent dry meals, fluids between meals, ginger if she wishes, and avoiding smells that trigger nausea; doxylamine-pyridoxine from today, raised to four tablets a day if needed; then a second drug (metoclopramide, promethazine, or ondansetron after counseling); PUQE-24 score, weight, pulse, blood pressure, and electrolytes at each visit; same-day review if she cannot keep fluids down for 24 hours or loses more than 5 percent of her pre-pregnancy weight
  • Maternal-fetal medicine consultation for a first pregnancy at 38 with moderate nausea and vomiting and early weight loss: escalation thresholds, aneuploidy screening and diagnostic options, preeclampsia prevention, tuberculosis risk, and the plan for the rest of the pregnancy
  • Aneuploidy screening offered to all, with diagnostic testing available: cell-free DNA from 10 weeks, a nuchal translucency scan at 11 to 14 weeks, or chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis; a detailed anatomy scan at 18 to 22 weeks
  • Tuberculosis screening with an interferon-gamma release assay because of tuberculosis deaths in her household; a shielded chest radiograph and treatment decisions only if it is positive
  • Mental health: PHQ-9 at intake and the EPDS in each trimester and after any admission, with support for the strain of severe vomiting and for anxiety rooted in family loss
  • Preeclampsia prevention: low-dose aspirin 81 mg at bedtime from 12 to 16 weeks until delivery if she has one high-risk or more than one moderate-risk factor (she has two: first pregnancy and age 35 or older); blood pressure at every visit
  • Admission for hyperemesis gravidarum: 0.9% saline with potassium chloride guided by daily electrolytes; thiamine 100 mg intravenously before any dextrose, then orally; magnesium replacement; ondansetron after counseling and an electrocardiogram; stop metoclopramide; refeeding precautions with phosphate and magnesium checks as eating resumes; weight-adjusted enoxaparin while admitted; discharge when she keeps fluids and food down
  • Thyroid: suppressed TSH with a mildly raised free T4 during hyperemesis is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis; no antithyroid drug; repeat TSH and free T4 at 16 to 18 weeks, and test for TSH-receptor antibodies only if it persists or signs of Graves disease appear
  • Monitoring while nausea and vomiting last: PUQE-24, weight, pulse, and blood pressure at every visit; electrolytes until stable on oral intake; liver tests if abnormal; mood each trimester; antiemetic side effects (drowsiness, restlessness or abnormal movements, constipation, palpitations)

resource.title: Charlotte Brontë synthetic care plan
resource.description: Prenatal care of a first pregnancy at 38 complicated by hyperemesis gravidarum, following ACOG Practice Bulletin 189 and RCOG Green-top Guideline 69 (2024): dating ultrasound; severity by the PUQE-24 score, weight, and hydration rather than urine ketones; electrolytes, magnesium, phosphate, liver tests, and thyroid tests with recognition of gestational transient thyrotoxicosis; stepwise antiemetics (doxylamine-pyridoxine, then metoclopramide, then ondansetron after counseling on the very small absolute risk of orofacial clefting); admission with intravenous saline and potassium, thiamine before any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, magnesium replacement, refeeding precautions, and weight-adjusted thromboprophylaxis; mental health screening with the PHQ-9 and EPDS; routine prenatal care at an advanced maternal age, with aneuploidy screening offered (cell-free DNA and nuchal translucency, with diagnostic testing available), low-dose aspirin for two moderate preeclampsia risk factors, and tuberculosis screening with an interferon-gamma release assay because of tuberculosis deaths in her household. The historical cause of her death is disputed and is recorded as conflicting retrospective claims, not decided by the modern episode.
